title: Compare and Contrast Common Networking Hardware Devices

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Networks use devices that route traffic, connect local systems, provide wireless access, organize cabling, filter traffic, deliver power, terminate provider connections, and give endpoints network access.
For this objective, recognize each device by its function and distinguish hardware that can look similar while doing different jobs.
bullets: Access points, patch panels, and firewalls
sections.callout: Route → switch → connect → organize → protect → power → terminate → interface.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When CompTIA describes what a networking device is doing, can you identify the hardware and separate it from similar devices?

sections.title: Routers
paragraphs: A router connects different networks and forwards traffic between them using IP addressing. A common example connects a local network to the internet.
sections.callout: Traffic must move from one IP network to another → router.

sections.title: Switches
paragraphs: A switch connects computers, printers, servers, access points, phones, and other devices inside a local area network. It forwards Ethernet traffic primarily using MAC addresses.
sections.callout: Several wired devices communicate on the same LAN → switch.

sections.title: Router vs. Switch

table.caption: Core traffic devices
rows: Connects devices within the same LAN

sections.callout: Switch = inside; router = between.

sections.title: Managed Switch
paragraphs: A managed switch allows administrators to configure and monitor VLANs, port settings, trunks, security features, and other switch behavior through management interfaces.
sections.callout: Need VLANs, monitoring, or port control → managed switch.

sections.title: Unmanaged Switch
paragraphs: An unmanaged switch provides simple plug-and-play Ethernet connectivity with little or no configuration.
sections.callout: Basic connectivity with no administrative configuration → unmanaged switch.

sections.title: Managed vs. Unmanaged Switch
sections.callout: Need control → managed; need simple connectivity → unmanaged.

sections.title: Access Points
paragraphs: A wireless access point (AP) provides wireless devices access to a wired network by bridging wireless clients into the LAN.
sections.callout: Add Wi-Fi coverage to an existing wired LAN → access point.

sections.title: Access Point vs. Router

table.caption: Combined consumer features, separate networking roles
rows: Provides wireless access to a LAN

sections.callout: Router routes; an AP provides Wi-Fi.

sections.title: Patch Panel
paragraphs: A patch panel is a central passive termination and organization point for permanent network cable runs. Short patch cables connect its front ports to active equipment such as switches.
sections.callout: Many building Ethernet runs terminate in one rack → patch panel.

sections.title: Patch Panel vs. Switch
sections.callout: Patch panel organizes; switch communicates.

sections.title: Firewall
paragraphs: A firewall allows or blocks traffic according to security rules based on factors such as source, destination, protocol, port, and policy. It can be hardware, software, or part of another appliance.
sections.callout: Permit or deny network traffic using security rules → firewall.

sections.title: Firewall vs. Router
sections.callout: Router moves traffic; firewall controls traffic.

sections.title: Power over Ethernet (PoE)
paragraphs: Power over Ethernet (PoE) carries electrical power and network data over Ethernet cabling, reducing the need for a separate endpoint power connection.
Wireless access points, IP cameras, VoIP phones, and other network devices commonly use PoE.
sections.callout: One Ethernet cable supplies data and power → PoE.

sections.title: PoE Injector
paragraphs: A PoE injector adds electrical power to an Ethernet connection when the existing switch does not provide PoE.
sections.callout: Existing non-PoE switch plus one powered endpoint → PoE injector.

sections.title: PoE Switch
paragraphs: A PoE switch provides Ethernet data and electrical power directly from its switch ports, simplifying deployments with many powered devices.
sections.callout: Many access points, phones, or cameras require centralized power → PoE switch.

table.caption: PoE delivery options
rows: Adds power to one or a few links from a non-PoE switch
Provides power directly from many switch ports

sections.title: PoE Standards

table.caption: Power over Ethernet generations
rows: Higher-power PoE, often called PoE++ or 4-pair PoE

paragraphs: Power capability increases across these generations. The switch or injector must support the connected device's power requirement.
sections.callout: af → at → bt = increasing power capability.

sections.title: Cable Modem
paragraphs: A cable modem terminates internet service delivered through a cable-provider network, commonly over coaxial cable, and connects that service to customer networking equipment.
sections.callout: ISP service enters through coax → cable modem.

sections.title: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)
paragraphs: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) provides internet connectivity over telephone copper wiring, typically through a DSL modem or gateway.
sections.callout: Traditional telephone copper carries internet service → DSL.

sections.title: Cable Modem vs. DSL
sections.callout: Coax = cable; phone line = DSL.

sections.title: Optical Network Terminal (ONT)
paragraphs: An Optical Network Terminal (ONT) terminates a fiber-optic provider connection at the customer premises and converts the optical signal for customer networking equipment.
sections.callout: Fiber internet enters the building → ONT.

sections.title: Cable Modem vs. DSL vs. ONT
sections.callout: Identify the physical provider medium first.

sections.title: Network Interface Card (NIC)
paragraphs: A Network Interface Card (NIC) gives a device the ability to connect to a network. It can be built in or added as an Ethernet, wireless, PCIe, or USB network adapter.
sections.callout: Computer needs network-interface hardware → NIC.

sections.title: Physical Media Access Control (MAC) Address
paragraphs: A physical Media Access Control (MAC) address identifies a network interface at the data-link layer and is associated with NIC hardware. It is commonly written as hexadecimal values such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.
sections.callout: Identify the physical interface on the local LAN → MAC address.

sections.title: MAC Address vs. IP Address

table.caption: Interface and logical addressing
rows: Identifies a network interface on the local network
Logical address used across IP networks

sections.callout: MAC = interface identity; IP = logical network location.

sections.title: NIC vs. MAC Address
sections.callout: NIC = the adapter; MAC = the adapter's address.

sections.title: Networking Hardware Map
bullets: Access point → wireless clients into a LAN
Patch panel → organize and terminate cable runs
PoE injector → add power to a link
PoE switch → power directly from switch ports
Cable modem → coax; DSL → telephone copper; ONT → fiber
NIC → network interface; MAC address → interface identifier

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Connect devices in one LAN → switch
Data and power over Ethernet → PoE
Add power to non-PoE link → injector
Coax ISP → cable modem; telephone copper → DSL; fiber → ONT

sections.title: Objective 2.5 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Devices can sit beside one another or share one consumer enclosure. The exam cares about function, not appearance.

entries.title: Router vs. Switch
paragraphs: Between networks → router; within one LAN → switch.

entries.title: Managed vs. Unmanaged
paragraphs: Configuration, VLANs, or monitoring require a managed switch; simple connectivity fits unmanaged.

entries.title: Router vs. Access Point
paragraphs: Routing between networks is the router role; providing Wi-Fi is the access-point role.

entries.title: Patch Panel vs. Switch
paragraphs: A patch panel passively terminates cables; a switch actively forwards frames.

entries.title: Router vs. Firewall
paragraphs: A router forwards; a firewall permits or denies.

entries.title: PoE Injector vs. PoE Switch
paragraphs: An injector adds power to a link; a PoE switch supplies power directly from its ports.

entries.title: Cable vs. DSL vs. ONT
paragraphs: Coax → cable modem; telephone copper → DSL; fiber → ONT.

entries.title: NIC vs. MAC
paragraphs: The NIC is hardware; the MAC address identifies that interface.

sections.callout: Ask whether the device is routing, switching, providing wireless, organizing, filtering, powering, terminating, or interfacing.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Wireless clients join wired LAN → access point
Structured cabling terminates in rack → patch panel
Ethernet carries data and power → PoE
Add PoE to one link → injector
Multiple powered switch ports → PoE switch
Coax → cable modem; phone line → DSL; fiber → ONT
Route → router; switch → switch; wireless → AP; organize → patch panel; protect → firewall; power → PoE; terminate → modem/ONT; interface → NIC
